Krakeb（Qraqeb）為體鳴樂器，發聲來自器身振動。來源指出其以鐵或鋼手工: The krakeb (qraqeb) is an idiophone: the sound comes from the body of the instrument vibrating. The source states that it is made by hand from iron or steel, and that the body consists of four small cymbals, two on each side, joined by a cord; the player usually holds one pair in each hand. Its region is North Africa / the Maghreb, and it is found in Morocco. Beyond the metal cymbals and the joining cord, the source does not state the materials of the other parts.
Qraqeb（krakeb）是北非馬格里布格納瓦音樂使用的鐵製小鈸，屬體鳴樂器，: The qraqeb (krakeb) is an iron small cymbal used in the Gnawa music of the Maghreb in North Africa, an idiophone whose sound comes from the body vibrating. It is built of four small cymbals, two on each side, joined by a cord and made by hand from iron or steel. The player holds one pair in each hand and strikes them together; the Gnawa style usually keeps them closed after the strike, while in Tunisia they are pulled quickly apart so that the ring sounds. They often carry the rhythm for the Gnawa musicians in spiritual music, can play alongside the sintir, and a group may have as many as twenty players.
Qraqeb（亦作 Krakeb）的發展與北非馬格里布地區的格納瓦音樂（Gnaw: The development of the qraqeb (also written krakeb) is closely tied to the Gnawa music of the Maghreb in North Africa, where it is mainly the rhythmic core. The origin of the name is unknown, and it is not found in standard Arabic with this meaning. Gnawa music carries the memory of sub-Saharan West Africans sold into Algeria, Morocco, Libya and Tunisia; the sound of the clappers is understood as the sound of hooves and shackles, and also stands for the bonds removed when a slave gained freedom. The way of playing differs within the Maghreb: the Gnawa style usually keeps them closed between strokes, while in Tunisia they are pulled quickly apart after the stroke to bring out the ring.
krakeb 主要出現在格納瓦音樂中，作為節奏聲部。格納瓦音樂屬於北非馬格里布文: The krakeb appears mainly in Gnawa music, as the rhythmic part. Gnawa music belongs to the culture of the Maghreb in North Africa and is described as spiritual music, tied to the historical memory of Algeria, Morocco, Libya and Tunisia. The usual line-up is one sintir (guimbri) with up to twenty krakeb players, sometimes accompanied by a hajhuj. When listening, note the different regional ways of playing: in the Gnawa style the krakeb stay closed between the two strokes, so that the clash stands out most; in the Tunisian way they are pulled quickly apart after the stroke, so that the ring is more obvious.

塔克西姆響板音色清脆明亮，具有金屬質感的銳利特徵。其高頻成分豐富，能夠穿透樂隊音: The taqsim clappers have a crisp, bright timbre with a sharp, metallic edge. They are rich in high frequencies and cut through an ensemble, producing a clear strike. The range is fairly concentrated in the middle and high frequencies, and a stroke gives a short, forceful sound. Because they sound by the idiophone principle, the resonance comes mainly from the clappers themselves and the tone is relatively clean, with no long tail. Compared with the soft, lingering sound of cymbals, the taqsim clappers are more direct and abrupt; compared with a xylophone they sound more metallic and cold. These qualities let them mark the rhythmic points effectively in Middle Eastern traditional music and add a rhythmic skeleton to an improvised taqsim section.

演奏者每手持一副克拉凱布（Krakeb），每副由繩索串起四片鐵製小鉸片，兩側各兩: The player holds one pair of krakeb in each hand, each pair being four small iron plates strung on a cord, two on each side. To sound them, both hands close together at the same time and the plates clash to produce the idiophone sound. In Gnawa music they are usually kept closed after the stroke, which makes the clash most obvious; in the Tunisian way they are pulled quickly apart after the stroke so that the ring stands out. A beginner can practise holding them steadily in one hand and closing both hands together in time, then choose whether to keep them closed or pull them apart according to the occasion, and keep the rhythm going.
